buildUp: Start from the idea of layers: you need a nozzle that squeezes out a thin, steady line of melted plastic, so a heater block melts filament and gears push it through at a measured rate.
The nozzle has to draw anywhere in a flat layer, so one motor moves the head left and right on steel rods and another slides the bed forwards and backwards beneath it.
After each layer it has to rise by a fraction of a millimetre, so two motors turn lead screws that lift the whole gantry evenly at both ends.
The whole print rests on its first layer, so the bed is heated, covered with a textured steel sheet the plastic grips, and checked by a probe that maps any unevenness.
Filament must stay solid until the very tip, or it jams, so a heat sink and fan keep the part above the heater cool, and a second fan cools each fresh layer so it sets before the next one lands.
Finally the brains and the instructions: a control board drives the motors and heaters, and slicing software turns a 3D model into G-code, thousands of simple movement commands.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Slice the object into hundreds of thin horizontal layers and build it from the bottom up, drawing each layer with a thin bead of melted plastic. A hard three-dimensional problem becomes a stack of easy two-dimensional drawings, and the machine only needs to move a nozzle precisely and squeeze out plastic at the right rate.

hardParts.title: A perfect first layer
hardParts.why: The first layer is only about 0.2 mm thick, so if the bed is a tenth of a millimetre too high the nozzle scrapes it, and too low the plastic won't stick. Beds are never perfectly flat, so the probe maps dozens of points and the printer adjusts the height continuously as it draws, while the heated, textured sheet holds the print down against the pull of shrinking plastic.

hardParts.title: Melting plastic in exactly one place
hardParts.why: The plastic must be fully molten in the nozzle at over 200 °C, yet stay solid a few millimetres above it so the gears can push it like a piston. If heat creeps upwards, the filament softens too early, swells and jams, so the hotend packs a sharp hot-to-cold change into a very short distance.

hardParts.title: Accuracy without feedback
hardParts.why: Because the controller only counts steps, it never checks where the head really is. If a motor misses steps after hitting a blob of plastic, or a belt is slack, every layer after that is shifted, so belts must be tight, motors strong enough, and accelerations limited.

principles.explanation: Each fresh bead of plastic briefly melts into the layer below and bonds as it cools, so a print holds together but is always weakest between its layers. Filaments like PLA and PETG are thermoplastics: long tangled molecules that slide past each other when hot and lock in place when cool, over and over, like candle wax. At around 200 °C or more, the hot bead softens the surface beneath it just enough for the molecules to mingle across the join. That bond is never quite as strong as the inside of a bead, like wood along its grain.
principles.title: Plastics that melt and set again

principles.explanation: The controller knows where the nozzle is without measuring it, because it just counts motor steps from a known starting point. A stepper motor turns in fixed steps, 200 to a turn, and the driver can split each into 16 smaller microsteps, giving 3,200 per turn. A 20-tooth pulley pulls a belt with 2 mm teeth about 40 mm per turn, so each microstep moves the head about 0.0125 mm, or 80 microsteps per millimetre.
principles.title: Counting steps instead of measuring

principles.explanation: Plastic shrinks as it cools, so each new layer pulls inwards on the cooler layer beneath it and can curl a print's corners off the bed unless the bed is heated. Most materials get smaller as they cool, and plastics shrink by a fraction of a percent between printing temperature and room temperature. Half a percent across a 200 mm part is a whole millimetre. A heated bed keeps the lower layers warm and lessens that pull.
principles.title: Plastic shrinks as it cools

principles.explanation: A printer can only go as fast as its hotend can melt plastic, so speed is capped by heat, not just by the motors. A line 0.4 mm wide and 0.2 mm tall drawn at 100 mm a second needs 8 cubic millimetres of plastic melted every second. A typical hotend can melt only somewhere around 10 to 15 cubic millimetres a second. That's also why big prints take so long: a 1 kg spool of PLA is about 800 cubic centimetres, over a day of nonstop printing at 8 cubic millimetres a second.
principles.title: Speed is limited by melting

firstPrinciples.problem: Turn a shape on a computer into a solid object on your desk, whatever the shape, without a workshop. Carving needs a different cut for every shape and moulding needs an expensive mould for each one; you want one cheap machine that can make anything, accurate to a fraction of a millimetre, out of a material that shrinks and warps as it cools.

questions.answer: Between layers. Each layer bonds to the one below only while the fresh plastic is hot, so those joins are weaker than the plastic within each layer.
questions.question: If you pull on a printed part, which way is it most likely to snap?

questions.answer: Each bead needs something underneath to land on. Gentle slopes work because each layer overlaps the one below, but a flat overhang needs removable supports printed beneath it.
questions.question: Why can't the printer draw a flat shelf sticking straight out into mid-air?

questions.answer: It moves each axis to a known end point when it starts, then counts every step it sends to the motors from there. Since each step is a fixed tiny distance, the count gives the position.
questions.question: How does the printer know where the nozzle is if it never measures it?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: For a 3D printer, complexity is almost free. A hollow lattice, an internal channel or a part that would need a ten-piece mould costs no more to print than a plain block, and often less, because the time depends on how much plastic you lay down, not on how intricate the shape is. That flips the usual rule of manufacturing, where every extra curve costs money, and it's why a machine built from simple rods, belts and stepper motors can make shapes no factory would attempt in small numbers.

name: 3D Printer
overview:
A 3D printer of this kind is a robot that draws with hot plastic. A reel of plastic filament feeds into the print head, where a pair of gears pushes it into a heated nozzle at around 200 to 260 °C. Molten plastic squeezes out of a hole about 0.4 mm wide, and the printer traces the outline and infill of one thin slice of the object, then moves up a fraction of a millimetre and draws the next slice on top.

Three sets of motors make that possible. One moves the print head left and right along a pair of steel rods, one slides the whole bed forwards and backwards beneath it, and two more turn lead screws that raise the gantry carrying the head, one layer at a time. These stepper motors move in tiny fixed steps, so the controller always knows exactly where the nozzle is without needing to measure it.

Getting the first layer to stick is the hardest part, so the bed is heated and covered with a removable textured steel sheet that flexes to pop prints off. A probe next to the nozzle taps the bed at several points before each print to map any unevenness, and the printer quietly compensates as it goes. The instructions come from slicing software, which turns a 3D model into thousands of lines of movement commands called G-code.

parts.description: Stiff aluminium frame standing across the middle that holds the Z axis and the gantry square to the bed.

details.didYouKnow: This single upright frame with a sliding bed grew out of the open-source RepRap project, started in 2005 at the University of Bath with the goal of a printer that could print many of its own parts.
details.howItWorks: The upright frame is the printer's backbone: the Z motors bolt to its foot, the lead screws and gantry rise in front of it, and it is fixed square across the base rails. If it leans or flexes even slightly, the nozzle drifts relative to the bed and layers stop lining up, so its stiffness shows directly in print quality. The big window in the middle keeps it light while leaving the strong outer ring to carry the load.
keyNumbers: Typically about 40 cm wide and 45 cm tall
Holds a build height of roughly 220 mm
Whole printer weighs about 7 kg
details.madeOf: Usually a single aluminium plate or a set of aluminium extrusions, cut and drilled by machine. Aluminium gives a good balance of stiffness, low weight and resistance to rust, and a single piece is easier to keep square than many bolted ones.

parts.name: Upright frame

parts.description: Pair of aluminium extrusions running front to back that form the base and carry the bed's guide rods.

details.didYouKnow: Slotted aluminium extrusion is used like a grown-up construction kit in factories, and hobbyists borrowed it to build hundreds of different home-made printer designs.
details.howItWorks: The two base rails run front to back and carry everything else: the upright frame bolts across them, the end plates close their ends, and the bed's smooth guide rods sit above them. Because the bed slides along this axis, the rails must be straight and parallel, or the bed will rock and bind as it moves. Slots along their length let parts be bolted on anywhere with sliding nuts.
keyNumbers: Typically about 30 to 40 cm long
Profile roughly 20 to 30 mm across
Shown as a mirrored pair: 2 rails
details.madeOf: Aluminium extrusions, made by pushing hot aluminium through a shaped die, rather like toothpaste from a tube. The hollow, ribbed profile gives a lot of stiffness for very little metal.

parts.name: Base rails

parts.description: Plates closing the ends of the base, holding the bed motor at the back and the idler pulley at the front.

details.didYouKnow: The belt tension between these two plates is often checked by plucking the belt like a guitar string; some makers even let you measure the note with a phone to set the tension.
details.howItWorks: The back plate holds the bed motor, and the front plate holds a free-spinning idler pulley, so the bed belt makes a long loop between them under the bed. Both plates also clamp the ends of the bed's guide rods, keeping them parallel and at the right height. They tie the two base rails together so the base stays a rigid rectangle.
keyNumbers: Shown as a mirrored pair: 2 plates
Guide rods typically 8 mm in diameter
Motor mounts on a hole pattern about 31 mm apart
details.madeOf: Aluminium plate, or sometimes tough printed plastic on budget machines. Metal is preferred where the motor and belt pull hardest, because it does not creep or soften over time.

parts.name: Front & back plates

parts.description: Turns mains electricity into 24 volts for the motors, heaters and control board.

details.didYouKnow: Many printers moved from 12 V to 24 V because, for the same power, twice the voltage needs only half the current, so wires and connectors run cooler and the heaters warm up faster.
details.howItWorks: The power supply takes mains electricity and turns it into a steady 24 volts of direct current. It does this with a switch-mode design: it chops the mains thousands of times a second, passes it through a small transformer, then smooths it out again. The heated bed and hotend draw most of the power, especially while warming up, with the motors and electronics taking the rest.
keyNumbers: Output typically 24 V DC
Rated roughly 150 to 300 W
Accepts mains of about 100 to 240 V
details.madeOf: A metal case around a circuit board with capacitors, a ferrite-cored transformer and power transistors. The metal case helps shed heat and keeps the mains wiring safely enclosed.

parts.name: Power supply

parts.description: The printer's computer: it reads G-code and drives the motors, heaters and fans, step by step.

details.didYouKnow: G-code dates back to the 1950s, when it was developed at MIT for computer-controlled milling machines. The firmware on most hobby printers is open source, so anyone can read and modify it.
details.howItWorks: The control board reads G-code commands one by one and turns them into precisely timed pulses for each motor, so all the axes move together along smooth lines and curves. It also runs temperature control loops for the hotend and bed, reads the probe, and switches the fans. Small stepper driver chips on the board turn the pulses into carefully shaped currents in the motor coils.
keyNumbers: Typically a 32-bit processor
Usually 5 or more stepper drivers
Microstepping up to about 256 steps per full step
Runs on 24 V
details.madeOf: A multi-layer circuit board carrying a 32-bit microcontroller, stepper driver chips, power transistors and connectors. Thick copper layers help carry heater current and pull heat away from the drivers.

parts.name: Control board

parts.description: Plastic box over the control board, with a fan to keep the motor drivers cool.

details.didYouKnow: On many open-source printers, a good share of the plastic parts, covers included, are themselves 3D printed, often on rows of identical printers in the maker's own print farm.
details.howItWorks: The cover shields the control board from dust, stray bits of filament and curious fingers, and keeps the mains-side wiring out of reach. A small fan pulls air across the stepper driver chips, which get warm when the motors work hard. If the drivers overheat, they protect themselves by cutting power, which can cause a print to shift sideways.
keyNumbers: Fan typically about 40 mm across
Fan runs on 24 V
Usually a wall roughly 2 to 3 mm thick
details.madeOf: Usually printed or injection-moulded plastic such as PETG or ABS. Plastic is light, insulates electrically and can be shaped around connectors and cable paths easily.

parts.name: Electronics cover

parts.description: Front screen and control knob for starting prints, changing filament and adjusting settings.

details.didYouKnow: Many printers can also be run over a network, so you can start a print from your computer and watch its progress on a phone without touching the knob at all.
details.howItWorks: The screen shows temperatures, progress and menus, while the knob scrolls through options when turned and selects when pressed. From here you can start a print from a USB stick or memory card, load and unload filament, and tweak speed or temperature mid-print. It talks to the control board over a short ribbon cable.
keyNumbers: Screen typically about 3 to 3.5 inches
Encoder clicks roughly 20 to 30 times per turn
Prints often run for several hours
details.madeOf: A small LCD panel and a rotary encoder on a circuit board, inside a plastic housing. A rotary encoder never reaches an end stop, so it can scroll through menus of any length.

parts.name: Display & knob

parts.description: Stepper motor at the back that pulls the bed forwards and backwards with a toothed belt.

details.didYouKnow: Because a sliding bed carries heavy, wobbly mass, tall thin prints can sway as the bed jerks back and forth, which is one reason some newer printers keep the bed still and move only the head.
details.howItWorks: The bed motor turns a small toothed pulley that grips the bed belt, pulling the bed carriage forwards or backwards. A stepper motor moves in fixed steps, so the controller knows where the bed is just by counting pulses, after a single trip to a limit switch at start-up. Because it has to move the whole bed and the print on it, this motor works harder than the X motor when changing direction.
keyNumbers: About 42 mm square (NEMA 17 size)
Typically 200 full steps per turn
A 20-tooth pulley moves the belt about 40 mm per turn
details.madeOf: A steel and aluminium body around copper coils and a permanent magnet rotor. The coils are energised in sequence to step the rotor round.

parts.name: Bed motor

parts.description: Rubber timing belt with glass-fibre strands inside, clamped under the bed carriage.

details.didYouKnow: The GT2 tooth has a rounded shape designed to roll in and out of the pulley cleanly, which reduces the backlash you would get with older square-toothed belts.
details.howItWorks: The belt runs from the motor pulley at the back to an idler pulley at the front, and both ends are clamped under the bed carriage. As the motor turns, the belt drags the carriage along with it. Its teeth mesh with the pulley so it cannot slip, keeping every step of the motor matched to a fixed distance of bed travel.
keyNumbers: Tooth pitch of 2 mm (GT2 profile)
Typically about 6 mm wide
Roughly 80 microsteps per mm of travel with 16x microstepping
details.madeOf: Rubber or polyurethane with glass-fibre strands running inside along its length. The rubber makes the teeth grip, while the fibre cords stop the belt stretching under tension.

parts.name: Bed belt

parts.description: Pair of smooth hardened steel rods, clamped to the end plates, that the bed carriage's linear bearings roll along.

details.didYouKnow: Some printers replace round rods with flat linear rails, where the balls run in machined grooves, because the rail can be bolted down along its whole length and never sags.
details.howItWorks: The bed carriage needs to glide front to back without rocking, so it rides on linear ball bearings that clamp round these two rods. The rods are held at each end by clamps on the front and back plates, which keep them parallel and level. Any bend or twist in them shows up directly as a bed that rocks or binds as it moves.
keyNumbers: Typically 8 mm in diameter
Roughly 30 to 40 cm long
Usually three or four bearings share the two rods
details.madeOf: Hardened carbon or stainless steel, ground round and polished, often with a hard chrome finish. A hard surface stops the bearing balls wearing grooves into the rods over many hours of printing.

parts.name: Bed guide rods

parts.description: Aluminium plate that slides on linear bearings and carries the heated bed.

details.didYouKnow: Linear ball bearings have rows of tiny balls that roll along the rod and then loop back through a return channel, so the carriage glides on rolling balls rather than sliding metal.
details.howItWorks: The bed carriage rides on linear ball bearings that slide along two smooth steel guide rods, so it can move front to back with very little friction or wobble. The belt clamps to its underside, and the heated bed sits on top, usually on adjustable spacers. Everything it carries moves with it, so keeping it light helps the printer change direction quickly.
keyNumbers: Guide rods typically 8 mm in diameter
Travel of roughly 210 mm front to back
Linear bearings about 15 mm across and 24 mm long
details.madeOf: Aluminium plate, cut and drilled by machine. Aluminium is light and stiff, and it does not warp as the heated bed above it warms and cools.

parts.name: Bed carriage

parts.description: Flat aluminium plate with a heater on its underside and magnets in it to hold the print sheet down.

details.didYouKnow: Magnets lose strength when they get hot, which is one reason these beds use special high-temperature magnets and do not go much above about 120 degrees C.
details.howItWorks: A heater on the underside warms the whole plate evenly, which helps the first layer stick and stops the corners of a print curling up as they cool. A temperature sensor tells the control board when to switch the heater on and off to hold the set point. Magnets set into the plate pull the spring-steel print sheet down flat, so it can be lifted off and snapped back in seconds.
keyNumbers: Heats up to about 110 to 120 degrees C
Typically about 60 degrees C for PLA
Print area of roughly 250 x 210 mm
Usually takes a few minutes to warm up
details.madeOf: An aluminium plate with a printed-circuit or silicone heater on the back and heat-tolerant magnets in it. Aluminium spreads heat well, so the surface stays an even temperature.

parts.name: Heated bed

parts.description: Removable spring-steel sheet with a textured coating; flex it and finished prints pop off.

details.didYouKnow: PETG can stick so well to a smooth PEI sheet that it tears pieces out of the coating, so people often add a thin layer of glue stick as a release agent.
details.howItWorks: The sheet is the surface the print is actually built on. Warm plastic sticks firmly to its coating, then lets go more easily as the sheet cools down. When the print is done, you lift the sheet off the magnetic bed and bend it slightly, and the stiff print pops free instead of having to be scraped off.
keyNumbers: Steel typically under 1 mm thick
About 250 x 210 mm print area
First layers usually about 0.2 mm thick
details.madeOf: Thin spring steel with a coating of PEI, a heat-resistant plastic, either as a smooth film or a textured powder coat. Spring steel can be flexed many times and always springs back flat.

parts.name: Print sheet

parts.description: Pair of stepper motors with lead screws that raise the whole gantry a fraction of a millimetre per layer.

details.didYouKnow: Z moves are tiny and slow compared with X and Y, so a stepper's holding force alone keeps the gantry in place even when the power is off.
details.howItWorks: The two Z motors sit at the foot of the upright frame, one each side, and turn the lead screws together so both ends of the gantry rise or fall by the same amount. After each layer they turn just a fraction of a revolution to lift the nozzle by one layer height. If one side slips out of step the gantry tilts, so printers often level it by driving both ends up against a stop.
keyNumbers: Shown as a mirrored pair: 2 motors
About 42 mm square (NEMA 17 size)
Typically 200 full steps per turn
Layer heights roughly 0.1 to 0.3 mm
details.madeOf: Stepper motors with a steel and aluminium body around copper coils, often with the lead screw built in as the motor's own shaft. Building in the screw removes a coupling that could wobble.

parts.name: Z motors

parts.description: Threaded steel rods turned by the Z motors; a nut in each X end climbs or descends as they turn.

details.didYouKnow: Many lead screws have several separate threads wound side by side, like stripes on a candy cane, so the nut travels further per turn while each groove stays small and strong.
details.howItWorks: Each lead screw passes through a nut held in an X end. As the screw turns, the nut cannot spin with it, so it is forced up or down the thread, carrying the gantry with it. The trapezoidal thread makes the screw strong and hard to turn backwards, so the weight of the gantry does not drive it down on its own.
keyNumbers: Shown as a mirrored pair: 2 screws
Typically 8 mm in diameter
Often about 8 mm of travel per turn
Roughly 25 to 30 cm long
details.madeOf: Rolled stainless or carbon steel, running in a brass or plastic nut. Steel against brass or plastic slides smoothly and wears slowly with a little grease.

parts.name: Z lead screws

parts.description: Printed blocks at each end of the gantry holding the rod ends, the lead-screw nuts and the X motor or pulley.

details.didYouKnow: The RepRap dream of a self-replicating machine is easiest to see here: parts like the X ends are the sort of thing a printer of this kind can print as spares for itself.
details.howItWorks: The X ends tie the gantry together: each one clamps the ends of both X rods and holds a nut riding on a Z lead screw. The left one also carries the X motor and the right one the idler pulley, so the X belt runs between them. They often slide on vertical guide rods too, which keeps the gantry from twisting as it rises.
keyNumbers: Shown as a mirrored pair: 2 X ends
Each clamps two 8 mm rods
Rods typically a few centimetres apart vertically
details.madeOf: Usually 3D printed or moulded tough plastic such as PETG. Printed parts can include the complex pockets for nuts, bearings and rods in a single piece.

parts.name: X ends

parts.description: Polished, hardened steel rod that the print head's bearings slide along, left to right.

details.didYouKnow: Hardening is done just on the surface, often by induction heating and quenching, so the rod gets a wear-resistant skin while its core stays tougher and less brittle.
details.howItWorks: The upper rod is one of the two tracks the print head slides along from left to right. Linear bearings in the carriage clamp around it, and because the two rods are spaced vertically, the pair stops the print head tipping forwards or backwards. The belt usually runs between or just beside the rods, close to the bearings, so the pull does not twist the head.
keyNumbers: Typically 8 mm in diameter
Roughly 35 to 40 cm long
Surface hardness typically about 60 on the Rockwell C scale
details.madeOf: Hardened steel, ground and polished very smooth and usually chrome plated. The hard surface is needed because the steel balls in the bearings would otherwise wear tracks into a softer rod.

parts.name: Upper X rod

parts.description: Polished, hardened steel rod that the print head's bearings slide along, left to right.

details.didYouKnow: A rod supported only at its ends sags most in the middle, and that sag grows very quickly with length, which is why longer printers move to thicker rods or rails mounted along their whole length.
details.howItWorks: The lower rod is the second track for the print head, nearer the nozzle. With the rod above, it forms a rigid ladder that resists the head's tendency to rock as it starts, stops and drags the nozzle over the print. A thin film of oil or grease keeps the bearings rolling quietly, and wiping away dust stops them crunching.
keyNumbers: Typically 8 mm in diameter
Head travel of roughly 250 mm
Bearings typically carry 4 rows of balls or more
details.madeOf: The same hardened, polished and often chrome-plated steel as the upper rod. Steel is far stiffer than aluminium, so a thin rod sags very little over the gantry's span.

parts.name: Lower X rod

parts.description: Stepper motor on the left X end that moves the print head left and right with a belt.

details.didYouKnow: Modern stepper drivers can sense the load on the motor from its electrical behaviour, so some printers find their home position by gently bumping into the end without needing a separate switch.
details.howItWorks: The X motor sits in the left X end and turns a toothed pulley that drives the X belt, pulling the print head left and right. Together with the bed motor it traces every outline and fill line of each layer. It rides up and down with the gantry, so its cable has to flex a little with every layer change.
keyNumbers: About 42 mm square (NEMA 17 size)
Typically 200 full steps, or 1.8 degrees, per step
16x microstepping gives about 3,200 microsteps per turn
details.madeOf: A stepper motor with a steel and aluminium body, copper coils and a permanent magnet rotor. Being part of the moving gantry, it is chosen to be compact and fairly light.

parts.name: X motor

parts.description: Toothed belt between the X motor and the idler pulley, clamped to the print head.

details.didYouKnow: A loose belt causes a tell-tale fault called ringing or ghosting, where faint ripples echo along the surface just after sharp corners.
details.howItWorks: The X belt loops from the motor pulley on the left X end to the idler pulley on the right, and its ends are clamped to the print head carriage. When the motor turns, the belt drags the head along the rods. It has to be tight enough not to bounce, but not so tight that it loads the bearings and motor shaft.
keyNumbers: Tooth pitch of 2 mm (GT2 profile)
Typically about 6 mm wide
A 20-tooth pulley moves it about 40 mm per turn
details.madeOf: Rubber or polyurethane reinforced with glass-fibre cords. The teeth grip the pulley, while the cords keep the belt from stretching so the head stops exactly where it should.

parts.name: X belt

parts.description: Carriage that slides on the X rods and holds the extruder, hotend, fan and probe.

details.didYouKnow: Firmware can measure how the print head vibrates and then shape its movements to cancel those vibrations, letting the printer run much faster without ringing.
details.howItWorks: The carriage is the platform for the whole print head. Bearings inside it ride on the two X rods, the belt clamps to it, and the extruder, hotend, fans and probe all bolt on. Keeping the nozzle close to the bearings and the whole assembly light helps the head stop sharply at corners without wobbling.
keyNumbers: Rides on two 8 mm rods
Speeds up to roughly 200 mm per second
Accelerations of several thousand mm per second squared
details.madeOf: Printed or moulded plastic, usually a tough, heat-resistant type such as PETG or ASA. It sits near a hot nozzle, so it must not soften at the warm temperatures around the hotend.

parts.name: Print head carriage

parts.description: Small motor and geared drive wheels that grip the filament and push it into the hotend.

details.didYouKnow: Before the head moves to a new spot, the extruder briefly pulls the filament back a little, called retraction, to relieve the pressure in the nozzle and reduce stringy hairs between parts.
details.howItWorks: A small stepper motor drives a pair of toothed wheels that pinch the filament from both sides and push it down into the hotend. Gears between the motor and the wheels multiply its force, so it can push firmly and stop precisely. Because the extruder sits right on top of the hotend (direct drive), there is only a short path for the filament, which makes it good at handling soft, rubbery filaments.
keyNumbers: Gear reductions roughly 3:1 to 10:1
Feeds 1.75 mm filament
Usually a few hundred motor steps per mm of filament
details.madeOf: A plastic housing with hardened steel drive wheels and steel or plastic gears, driven by a compact stepper motor. Hardened wheels keep their bite even with gritty, filled filaments.

parts.name: Extruder

parts.description: Finned cold end that keeps the filament solid until it reaches the hot zone, cooled by its own fan.

details.didYouKnow: If the heat sink fan fails, the filament softens too high up and swells in the tube, a problem called heat creep that can jam the extruder solid.
details.howItWorks: Between the cold extruder and the hot heater block sits a short, thin-walled tube called a heat break, which lets as little heat as possible creep upwards. The finned heat sink around it, cooled by a fan, carries away the heat that does get through. That keeps the filament stiff until the last moment so the extruder can push it like a piston.
keyNumbers: Fan typically about 30 to 40 mm
Fan usually runs whenever the hotend is above about 50 degrees C
Hot zone up to roughly 290 degrees C just below
details.madeOf: Aluminium fins, which conduct heat well and are easy to machine, around a steel, titanium or bimetal heat break. Those heat break materials conduct heat poorly, which is exactly what is wanted there.

parts.name: Hotend heat sink

parts.description: Aluminium block with a heater cartridge and temperature sensor that melts the plastic.

details.didYouKnow: Many hotend sensors are thermistors, resistors whose resistance drops sharply as they get hotter, so the board can work out the temperature just by measuring a resistance.
details.howItWorks: A cylindrical heater cartridge and a temperature sensor slot into holes in the block, and the nozzle screws into its bottom. The control board reads the sensor many times a second and pulses power to the heater to hold the target temperature within a degree or two, using a control method called PID. Firmware also watches for runaway heating and shuts everything down if the temperature does not respond as expected.
keyNumbers: Heater typically about 40 to 60 W
Up to roughly 290 degrees C
About 200 to 220 degrees C for PLA, 230 to 250 for PETG
details.madeOf: Usually aluminium, sometimes brass or copper for higher temperatures, wrapped in a silicone sock. The sock keeps heat in and stops the part cooling fan from chilling the block.

parts.name: Heater block

parts.description: Brass nozzle that the molten plastic squeezes out of, through a hole about 0.4 mm wide.

details.didYouKnow: Scott Crump filed his patent for fused deposition modelling in 1989, reportedly inspired by making a toy frog for his daughter with a glue gun; the patent's expiry around 2009 helped cheap home printers take off.
details.howItWorks: The nozzle screws into the heater block and narrows the molten plastic down to a fine stream. The printer usually lays a line slightly wider than the hole, and layers are kept thinner than the hole so each one is squashed onto the one below for good bonding. Its flat tip also smooths the top of each line as it passes.
keyNumbers: Hole about 0.4 mm as standard
Other sizes typically 0.25 to 0.8 mm
Layers usually up to about three quarters of the hole size
Commonly an M6 thread
details.madeOf: Brass, which conducts heat well and is easy to machine. Abrasive filaments filled with carbon fibre or glow-in-the-dark powder wear brass away quickly, so hardened steel or tipped nozzles are used for those.

parts.name: Nozzle

parts.description: Blower that aims cool air just below the nozzle so each layer sets before the next one goes on.

details.didYouKnow: For ABS, too much cooling makes layers shrink unevenly and split apart, so it is often printed with the fan barely on, or inside an enclosure to keep the air warm.
details.howItWorks: The part cooling fan blows through a duct aimed just below the nozzle, so freshly laid plastic sets quickly. This keeps overhangs from drooping, lets bridges span gaps in mid-air, and stops small details turning into a soft blob. The control board sets its speed layer by layer, often leaving it off for the first layer to help it stick.
keyNumbers: Blower typically about 50 mm across
Runs on 24 V
Usually full speed for PLA, much lower for PETG or ABS
details.madeOf: A plastic radial blower with a small brushless motor, plus a printed or moulded duct. A blower pushes air harder through a narrow duct than an ordinary flat fan would.

parts.name: Part cooling fan

parts.description: Sensor beside the nozzle that measures the bed at many points so the printer can correct for any tilt or bumps.

details.didYouKnow: Inductive probes drift as they warm up, so some printers measure the probe's own temperature and correct for it, otherwise the first layer would change between a cold and a warm start.
details.howItWorks: Before a print, the printer lowers the probe onto a grid of points across the bed and records the height at each one, building a map of tilt and bumps. During the print, the firmware nudges the Z axis up and down as the head moves, so the first layer stays an even thickness everywhere. Some probes sense the metal sheet by induction without touching it; others use a load cell that feels the nozzle itself touch the bed.
keyNumbers: Typically probes a grid of dozens of points
First layer usually about 0.2 mm thick
Inductive probes sense metal a few millimetres away
details.madeOf: Electronics in a plastic body: an inductive probe has a small coil whose magnetic field changes near metal, while a load cell uses strain gauges bonded to a metal beam that bends very slightly under force.

parts.name: Bed probe

parts.description: Reel of plastic filament, usually 1.75 mm thick: PLA for everyday prints, PETG or ABS for tougher parts.

details.didYouKnow: Some filaments, especially nylon and PETG, absorb moisture from the air, which then boils in the nozzle and causes popping, stringing and rough surfaces, so they are stored with drying sachets or dried before use.
details.howItWorks: The spool stores the filament wound in neat layers so it unwinds smoothly as the extruder pulls on it. It turns freely on the spool holder, and as it empties it spins faster for the same feed rate. A tangled or badly wound spool can snag and stop the filament feeding, ruining a print partway through.
keyNumbers: Typically holds about 1 kg of filament
About 330 m of 1.75 mm PLA per kilo
Spool roughly 200 mm across
details.madeOf: Usually moulded plastic or recycled cardboard. Cardboard spools cut down on plastic waste but need a dry place, since damp cardboard can shed dust.

parts.name: Filament spool

parts.description: Rod on top of the frame that the spool spins on as filament is pulled off.

details.didYouKnow: Because a spool holder is so simple, it is one of the most popular first things people design and print for themselves, and thousands of variants are shared online.
details.howItWorks: The holder gives the spool an axle to turn on, high up so the filament can drop down to the extruder without sharp bends. Mounting it on top of the frame keeps the printer compact. Any drag here adds to the force the extruder must pull with, so smooth turning helps avoid under-extrusion.
keyNumbers: Carries a full spool of about 1.2 kg including the reel
Spool hub hole typically around 50 mm
Sits roughly 50 cm above the desk
details.madeOf: A metal or plastic rod or bracket fixed to the top of the frame. Some include small ball bearings so even a heavy, full spool turns with little resistance.

parts.name: Spool holder

parts.description: The plastic 'ink': a solid strand pulled into the extruder, melted, and laid down as a thin bead.

details.didYouKnow: Early RepRap printers mostly used thicker 3 mm filament; the thinner 1.75 mm size later became the standard because it is easier to push accurately and melts faster.
details.howItWorks: The filament is both the material and, below its melting point, the piston: the extruder pushes the solid strand, which forces the molten plastic ahead of it out of the nozzle. The printer controls how much plastic comes out by controlling exactly how far the filament is pushed. Each layer is a bead of melted plastic fused onto the one beneath it.
keyNumbers: Typically 1.75 mm thick
Diameter usually held within about 0.02 to 0.05 mm
PLA prints at about 200 to 220 degrees C
PETG at about 230 to 250 degrees C
details.madeOf: Thermoplastics such as PLA, PETG, ABS or flexible TPU, which soften when heated and harden again when cool. PLA is made from plant starch and is easy to print; PETG and ABS are tougher and handle more heat.

parts.name: Filament

summary: A desktop 3D printer: it melts plastic filament in a hot nozzle and draws an object one thin layer at a time, with stepper motors moving the nozzle left and right and up, and the bed front and back.
